meta.title: Semantic Kernel Overview
meta.thesis: Semantic Kernel Overview is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: An enterprise copilot uses Semantic Kernel plugins for CRM, calendar, and knowledge-base actions. By the end, they should be able to build or review Semantic Kernel plugin plan with functions and planners, measure plugin calls remain auditable and permissioned, and catch the failure where the planner composes a high-risk action without policy checks.

modules.title: Separate Semantic Kernel from Agent Framework
modules.summary: Semantic Kernel and Agent Framework solve related but different moments.
objectives: Define Microsoft Agent Framework as newer production path.

blocks.title: The Microsoft stack has layers and eras

spans.text: Problem anchor: a learner finds an old Semantic Kernel plugin tutorial and a new Microsoft Agent Framework workflow sample. Both are Microsoft agent material, but they teach different abstractions and production paths.

Semantic Kernel centers kernels, model services, plugins, functions, planners, memory, and agents in app code. Microsoft Agent Framework is positioned for newer production agents, workflows, state, middleware, telemetry, and .NET/Python parity.
Always say whether the example is SK, Agent Framework, Foundry-hosted, or AutoGen-era.

blocks.analogy: Do not file every Microsoft agent sample in the same drawer.

blocks.title: Case study: existing SK plugin app

spans.text: An enterprise already has SK plugins wrapping CRM and document search. A lesson should explain the kernel/plugin model instead of pretending the app is greenfield Agent Framework.
A new agent workflow with human approval, telemetry, and Azure hosting may be better framed with Microsoft Agent Framework.

items.text: Identify existing codebase and package family.
State whether the design is migration or greenfield.

blocks.title: Naming clarity
blocks.prompt: Why distinguish Semantic Kernel from Microsoft Agent Framework?

options.text: They emphasize different abstractions and production paths in Microsoft’s agent ecosystem.

blocks.explanation: Naming clarity prevents wrong implementation choices.

modules.title: Kernel and plugins expose callable skills
modules.sub: Semantic Kernel organizes model services and functions in app code.
modules.summary: The kernel wires model services and callable functions.
objectives: Define kernel, plugins, and native/prompt functions.

blocks.title: Plugins are the SK tool surface

spans.text: In Semantic Kernel, application code registers model services and plugins with the kernel. Plugins can wrap native code functions, prompt functions, OpenAPI functions, MCP tools, or other capabilities.
Automatic function choice is useful, but plugin descriptions, schemas, auth, and side-effect classification still matter. The app owns security and evaluation.
A plugin function should have a narrow name, description, input schema, and failure behavior.

blocks.analogy: The kernel is the workbench; plugins are the labeled tools hanging above it.

cells.text: Broad authority if function is vague.
Permissions and auth need host policy.

blocks.title: Plugin contract
blocks.prompt: What should every plugin function define?

options.text: A hidden global admin token in the prompt.
A narrow purpose, input contract, auth/side-effect assumptions, and failure behavior.

modules.title: Agent Framework adds workflows, middleware, and telemetry
modules.sub: Newer Microsoft agent work looks like production app infrastructure.
modules.summary: Agent Framework is the newer Microsoft workflow-oriented layer.
objectives: Name Agent, Workflow, middleware, state, and telemetry.
Compare with LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK.

blocks.title: Agent Framework is more workflow-shaped

spans.text: Microsoft Agent Framework combines agents and workflows with sequential, concurrent, branching, handoff, and group collaboration patterns. It also emphasizes middleware, telemetry, state/checkpoints, and integration with Microsoft hosting and identity.
Use it when the surrounding system is Microsoft-heavy: Azure OpenAI, Foundry, Microsoft 365, .NET services, enterprise identity, OpenTelemetry, or durable hosting.
If provider-neutral graph control matters more than Microsoft integration, compare LangGraph carefully.

blocks.analogy: Agent Framework is a production floor, not just a plugin shelf.

spans.text: A compliance assistant runs research, review, human approval, and publish steps inside Azure-hosted infrastructure. Agent Framework can express agents and workflow steps while telemetry flows into the Microsoft stack.
A small notebook demo with one function call may not need that layer.

items.text: Add middleware for policy and telemetry.

blocks.title: Agent Framework fit
blocks.prompt: When is Microsoft Agent Framework especially plausible?

options.text: When the app is a one-line string formatter.
When the team needs Microsoft ecosystem integration, workflows, middleware, telemetry, and .NET/Python support.
When no workflow or tools exist.

blocks.explanation: Fit follows ecosystem and production workflow needs.

modules.title: Code the plugin/workflow idea in one slice
modules.sub: A small example should show agent, tool, review, and workflow relation.
modules.summary: The code should reveal roles and review points.
objectives: Avoid claiming one API fits all languages and versions.

spans.text: Microsoft docs and samples vary by package, language, and version. A lesson can show the production shape while warning learners to check current SDK signatures before copying.
Spaced recall: from choosing frameworks, prototype the riskiest slice. For Microsoft stack, that may be identity, telemetry, or workflow approval.
Label code as pseudocode when it abstracts over preview or language-specific APIs.

blocks.title: Microsoft Agent Framework-style workflow sketch
blocks.code:
# Pseudocode: check current Microsoft Agent Framework SDK signatures before copying.
class Agent:
    def __init__(self, name, tools=None):
        self.name = name
        self.tools = tools or []

def search_kb(topic):
    return f"grounded notes for {topic}"

researcher = Agent("researcher", tools=[search_kb])
reviewer = Agent("reviewer")

workflow = [
    ("research", researcher.name),
    ("review", reviewer.name),
    ("human_approval", "required before publish"),
]
print(workflow)
blocks.explanation: The sketch teaches the workflow shape without pretending every current SDK has identical syntax across languages and versions.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict which step requires human approval.
predictThenReveal.answer: The `human_approval` step explicitly gates publish after research and review.

blocks.title: Version-aware code
blocks.prompt: Why label some Microsoft examples as pseudocode?

options.text: SDK packages and language-specific APIs can differ, so learners should check current signatures.

blocks.explanation: Version clarity is part of accurate teaching.

modules.title: Plan migration and enterprise operations
modules.sub: Microsoft stack choices affect identity, telemetry, hosting, and support.
modules.summary: The overview ends with governance and migration discipline.
objectives: Verify telemetry and Responsible AI controls.

spans.text: Do not casually rewrite SK or AutoGen systems into Agent Framework without checking plugin parity, state shape, tool auth, telemetry, deployment, human review, and evals. A working demo is not a migration plan.
Azure examples may assume Azure identity, Foundry, Microsoft 365, or Durable Task. Call those assumptions out when teaching provider-neutral concepts.
A migration plan should include rollback and side-by-side evals.

blocks.title: Verify AI output from Microsoft agent stack

spans.text: Review the framework layer and operational assumptions.

items.text: The lesson distinguishes SK, Agent Framework, AutoGen, Foundry, and M365 agents where relevant.
Plugin/tool permissions, schemas, and side-effect classes are explicit.
Workflow state, middleware, telemetry, and human approval are tested.
Azure or Microsoft 365 assumptions are named rather than implied.
Migration plans compare feature parity, eval results, and rollback path.

blocks.title: Migration risk
blocks.prompt: What should block a casual SK-to-Agent-Framework rewrite?

options.text: Unverified feature parity, state shape, telemetry, tool permissions, or deployment assumptions.

framework.label: Framework
framework.laymanDefinition: A library or platform that provides agent building blocks and conventions.
framework.technicalNote: Framework choice affects state handling, tools, tracing, deployment model, ecosystem fit, and how much control the application keeps.

graph.label: Graph
graph.laymanDefinition: A workflow shape where nodes and edges define how work moves between steps.
graph.technicalNote: Graph-based agents make branching, retries, checkpoints, and human review more explicit than a single loose loop.

checkpoint.label: Checkpoint
checkpoint.laymanDefinition: A saved workflow state that lets execution resume or be inspected later.
checkpoint.technicalNote: Checkpoints are essential for durable agents because retries, approvals, and debugging need the exact state at a step boundary.

handoff.label: Handoff
handoff.laymanDefinition: Passing work from one agent, tool, or human role to another.
handoff.technicalNote: Handoffs need a typed payload, ownership transfer, stop condition, and audit trail so context does not vanish between actors.

sdk.label: SDK
sdk.laymanDefinition: A software development kit with APIs and helpers for building applications.
sdk.technicalNote: Agent SDKs encode assumptions about models, tools, sessions, tracing, and deployment, so evaluate those assumptions against the product architecture.

orchestration.label: Orchestration
orchestration.laymanDefinition: Coordinating steps, agents, tools, state, and decisions in a workflow.
orchestration.technicalNote: Orchestration owns sequencing, parallelism, retries, timeouts, approvals, and failure visibility across the agent system.
